opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most exciting open questions right now, and honestly the results we've been seeing have surprised even me. If you'd asked me ten years ago whether a classical learning system, essentially a neural network running on ordinary hardware, could model something like turbulent fluid flow or weather, I'd probably have said that's the kind of thing you need either brute-force simulation or maybe quantum computers for. These are highly nonlinear and chaotic, with huge state spaces.

But what we're finding, with things like our weather work and plasma control for fusion, is that nature seems to have a lot of structure in it. Even systems that look intractably complex tend to lie on some lower-dimensional manifold, and a learning system can discover and exploit it. It doesn't have to enumerate every possibility; it learns to model the dynamics efficiently, often far faster than traditional numerical solvers and in some cases more accurately.

I've started to wonder whether there's a general principle here: any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. That's a conjecture, not a proven result, but it would have deep implications for what's computable in practice, and even for complexity theory, the P versus NP kind of questions, framed in terms of physical systems.

Fluids are a great test case. The Navier-Stokes equations are notoriously hard, mathematically and computationally. If learned models can capture their behavior well enough to be useful, for climate modeling, aerodynamics, or keeping plasma stable in a tokamak, that's a big practical win. Scientifically, it suggests these systems aren't as random as they look. There's an underlying order, and learning systems may be the right tool to uncover it.

r001.rationale: It calls the Navier–Stokes equations mathematically and computationally hard, but does not identify singularities as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says classical learning systems have surprised the speaker by modeling turbulent fluid flow and could capture fluid behavior usefully.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fascinating open questions, actually, and it's something we think about a lot. Fluid dynamics, turbulence, the Navier-Stokes equations, these are sort of the canonical examples of chaotic, highly nonlinear systems where the traditional approach, which is numerical simulation, becomes enormously expensive the moment you want fine resolution. You're essentially bottlenecked by compute, and the errors compound.

And what we've seen, I think first with things like weather, with GraphCast and then the models that followed, is that learning systems can do something quite surprising. Weather is fundamentally a fluid dynamics problem, the atmosphere is a fluid, and yet a learned model trained on decades of reanalysis data can outperform the best physics-based numerical models on medium-range forecasting, and do it in under a minute on a single chip rather than hours on a supercomputer. That was a genuine moment for me, because it suggests that even for chaotic systems there's a lot of exploitable structure, there are regularities in the dynamics that the system learns to compress, even if we can't write them down analytically.

Now I'd be careful about what that means. I don't think these systems are discovering some hidden closed-form solution to turbulence. What they're doing is learning a very good approximation of the statistical behaviour of the system within the distribution they've seen. And the honest limitation is that chaotic systems have this exponential sensitivity, so beyond a certain horizon, prediction in the strict sense becomes impossible for any system, classical or learned. The question becomes about the quality of the probabilistic forecast, the ensemble, rather than a single trajectory.

Where I think it gets really interesting is the hybrid approach. Combining the learned components with the physical constraints, so conservation laws, symmetries, the things we know must hold, baked into the architecture or the loss. That's the direction I'm most excited about, because you get the speed and the pattern recognition of the learned system, but anchored by physics so it doesn't drift into nonsense out of distribution. And then of course the longer-term dream, which goes back to what I've always wanted to do with AI, is using these systems not just to simulate but to help us actually understand. To find the hidden structure in turbulence that we as humans haven't been able to see. I think that's plausible in the next decade or so, and it would be a wonderful example of AI being used for science.

r001.rationale: The response discusses computational cost, compounding errors, and chaos, but does not identify singularities as an obstacle to prediction.

r002.rationale: It says learned models can exploit structure in fluid dynamics and cites GraphCast outperforming physics-based models on medium-range weather forecasts.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s enormous potential, but we have to be precise about what we mean by prediction. With a turbulent fluid, you can have equations that describe the system very well, and yet tiny differences in the initial conditions lead to very different trajectories. A learning system doesn’t magically remove that sensitivity.

What it might do is learn a very useful approximation to the dynamics, so you can simulate things much faster, or predict statistical properties without tracking every little eddy. And often those are the properties you actually care about.

The approach I find particularly interesting is combining learning with the physics we already know. You don’t want the system to have to rediscover conservation laws from examples if you can build those constraints into it. Then it can concentrate on the parts that are computationally expensive or difficult to model.

The big question is whether it’s learned something that generalizes. Does it still work when you change the conditions, or move into a regime it hasn’t seen before? That’s where you need very careful testing. There’s a difference between producing something that looks like a plausible fluid and predicting what that particular fluid will actually do.

r001.rationale: It discusses sensitivity to initial conditions in turbulent fluids, but does not identify singularities as an obstacle to prediction.

r002.rationale: It says learning systems have “enormous potential” and may approximate fluid dynamics usefully, including faster simulation and prediction of statistical properties.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s enormous potential there. Fluids are a fascinating example because the underlying equations can be relatively compact, yet the behavior they produce is extraordinarily complex. And that’s an interesting setting for machine learning: can you learn enough of the structure to make useful predictions much faster than a conventional simulation?

The distinction I’d make is between predicting an exact trajectory and predicting the statistical properties of the system. In a chaotic system, a tiny error in the initial conditions can grow very rapidly. Learning doesn’t magically remove that limitation. But you may still be able to predict large-scale patterns, distributions, or quantities that matter for an engineering problem.

I suspect the most powerful approaches will combine learning with what we already know about the physics. You don’t want a model that merely produces something that looks like a fluid; you want it to respect conservation laws and behave sensibly under conditions it hasn’t seen before. If we can achieve that reliably, these systems could become incredibly useful scientific tools.

r001.rationale: The response discusses chaos and errors in initial conditions, but does not identify singularities as an obstacle to mathematical prediction.

r002.rationale: It says machine learning has “enormous potential” for fluids and could make useful predictions much faster than conventional simulation, communicating that learning systems may be highly capable in this area.
